cards.q: What is Telnet and its fundamental security problem?
cards.a: Telnet is a legacy remote-access protocol that uses TCP 23 to provide a virtual terminal session but does not encrypt the session; commands, session data, and authentication information can be captured, so SSH should be used instead.

cards.q: What are the protocol basics of Telnet?
cards.a: Telnet uses TCP 23, provides no encryption, uses the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) abstraction for a bidirectional text-based session, and on Cisco devices runs over the VTY lines for remote CLI access.

cards.q: What risks does an unencrypted Telnet session expose?
cards.a: Eavesdropping of session data, credential exposure, session hijacking, man-in-the-middle interception/modification, and compliance risk; the fundamental problem is the lack of encryption.

cards.q: How is Telnet permitted on Cisco VTY lines?
cards.a: With line vty 0 15, transport input telnet, login, and a password; note the VTY range varies by platform.

cards.q: What are the transport input options?
cards.a: transport input telnet permits Telnet only, transport input ssh permits SSH only, transport input all permits all supported protocols, and transport input none disables incoming remote-access protocols.

cards.q: Which command prevents Telnet while allowing SSH on the VTY lines?
cards.a: transport input ssh on those VTY lines blocks Telnet connections and permits only SSH.

cards.q: How is Telnet restricted with an ACL, and its limitation?
cards.a: An access-class such as access-class MGMT in attached to the VTY lines restricts which source addresses can connect; this provides access control but does not encrypt Telnet.

cards.q: How do Telnet and SSH compare?
cards.a: Both provide remote CLI access over VTY lines, but Telnet is TCP 23 without encryption and is not recommended, while SSH is TCP 22 with encryption and secure authentication.

cards.q: What commands manage Telnet sessions on a Cisco device?
cards.a: telnet <host> initiates a session, show users shows connected users including VTY sessions, show line shows terminal lines, show sessions shows outbound sessions, and exit or disconnect ends a session.

cards.q: Why would a Telnet connection be refused versus timing out?
cards.a: Refused means Telnet is not permitted on the VTY lines (check show running-config | section line vty); timeout usually means TCP 23 is blocked or unreachable (check routing, ACL, firewall).

cards.q: Do access-class and SSH solve the same problem?
cards.a: No. An access-class (ACL) restricts which management sources may connect, while SSH protects the session with encryption; they solve different security problems and are best combined.

cards.q: How do the common remote-access ports compare?
cards.a: Telnet = TCP 23, SSH = TCP 22, FTP control = TCP 21, and DNS = UDP/TCP 53; Telnet and SSH are the two remote CLI protocols to contrast.

cards.q: Does access-class MGMT in encrypt Telnet?
cards.a: No. access-class restricts which source addresses can reach the VTY lines; it does not encrypt the traffic, so Telnet remains vulnerable even when ACL-restricted.

cards.q: Are Cisco devices always SSH-enabled and Telnet-disabled by default?
cards.a: Not universally. SSH must be properly configured for secure remote management, and Telnet should be explicitly disabled or restricted; do not assume a default.

cards.q: What is the One-Minute Telnet memory?
cards.a: TELNET = TCP 23 + no encryption; it offers unencrypted remote terminal access over VTY lines, transport input ssh prevents Telnet on those lines, and SSH on TCP 22 is the secure replacement.
